title: A bivalent Lassa virus mRNA vaccine protects guinea pigs from lethal infection with Lassa virus

analysis.research_question_and_background: Lassa virus (LASV), the causative agent of the life-threatening febrile disease, Lassa fever, remains a major public health concern in West Africa, where hundreds of thousands of infections occur annually. However, no licensed vaccine is currently available, highlighting the urgent need for effective preventive measures.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Using a lethal CBA/N mouse model of infection with ML29, an LASV live-attenuated vaccine candidate encoding LASV GPC and NP, we evaluated the efficacy of an mRNA-LNP vaccine expressing LASV nucleoprotein (NP; LASnp-mRNA-LNP) and a bivalent vaccine combining LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP.
analysis.methods: We identified LASV GPC- and NP-derived CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell epitope peptides in CBA/N mice and demonstrated that vaccination induced robust antigen-specific T-cell responses.
analysis.main_results: We found that LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP each conferred protection in the absence of detectable neutralizing antibody responses. Importantly, the bivalent vaccine provided complete protection against lethal challenge with doses at which monovalent vaccines failed to protect all mice.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings establish LASV NP, in addition to GPC, as a protective antigen in the mRNA vaccine platform and provide a rationale for developing bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccines to improve protection against Lassa fever.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide a rationale for developing bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccines to improve protection against Lassa fever and suggest potential dose-sparing benefits in vaccine formulations.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was conducted in mice and guinea pigs, which may limit generalisability to humans. The evidence is moderate, as the findings are based on animal models and not yet validated in human trials.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates the efficacy of a bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccine against Lassa virus (LASV) in animal models. The research highlights the protective potential of both LASV glycoprotein precursor (GPC) and nucleoprotein (NP) antigens in the mRNA vaccine platform. The bivalent vaccine demonstrated complete protection against lethal LASV infection in guinea pigs, even at lower doses than monovalent vaccines. These findings support the development of bivalent vaccines for improved protection against Lassa fever. However, the study was conducted in animal models, which may limit its direct applicability to humans. The evidence is moderate, as the results are based on experimental models rather than clinical trials.

title: A transgenic Syrian hamster model for New World hemorrhagic fever mammarenavirus infection

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the need for a small-animal model to investigate New World hemorrhagic fever mammarenaviruses, which pose significant public health risks due to limited countermeasures.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study developed an hTfR1 knock-in golden Syrian hamster line to model Junín virus (JUNV) infection, focusing on the role of human transferrin receptor 1 (hTfR1) in viral entry.
analysis.methods: The researchers used transgenic techniques to introduce hTfR1 into Syrian hamsters and assessed their susceptibility to JUNV infection through viral entry and disease progression.
analysis.main_results: The hTfR1 knock-in hamsters were found to be susceptible to JUNV infection, supporting the role of hTfR1 in viral entry and providing a novel model for studying NWM pathogenesis.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study interpreted the findings as supporting TfR1-mediated entry as an essential step in JUNV pathogenesis and provided a new small-animal model for developing therapies against NWMs.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings could advance the development of host receptor-directed therapies and direct-acting antivirals to improve outcomes in patients with severe NWM infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study acknowledges the limitations of using a non-human model and the need for further validation in human-relevant contexts.

analysis.summary_en: This study developed an hTfR1 knock-in golden Syrian hamster model to investigate Junín virus (JUNV) infection, supporting the role of hTfR1 in viral entry and providing a new model for developing therapies against New World hemorrhagic fever mammarenaviruses.

title: Co-Infection of Lassa Fever-Malaria (LF) in Endemic Settings: Influence on LF Case Detection in Health Facilities in Ondo State, Nigeria

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to assess the influence of malaria co-infection on Lassa fever (LF) case detection in health facilities in Ondo State, Nigeria, where both diseases are endemic.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A convergent mixed-methods design was used, combining retrospective review of 463 LF and malaria records from 2021 to 2023 across 10 purposively selected facilities in five high-burden LGAs, alongside nine key-informant interviews.
analysis.methods: Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and logistic regression, while qualitative findings were analyzed thematically and integrated through a joint display.
analysis.main_results: Of the 463 records, 297 (64.1%) had positive results for both Lassa fever and malaria. Malaria positivity was associated with missed LF suspicion (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 5.30, 95% CI 2.13–13.19; p < 0.001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study suggests that malaria positivity may mask LF rather than establish an independent cause of mortality, highlighting the need for parallel assessment in co-infection scenarios.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings inform the development of diagnostic algorithms and surveillance strategies to improve LF detection in areas where malaria is prevalent.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on retrospective records and interviews, which may introduce recall bias. The evidence is moderate in strength due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the impact of malaria co-infection on Lassa fever (LF) case detection in health facilities in Ondo State, Nigeria. Using a mixed-methods approach, it combines quantitative analysis of 463 LF and malaria records with qualitative insights from interviews. The results show that 64.1% of the records had positive results for both diseases, and malaria positivity was strongly associated with missed LF suspicion. The authors interpret these findings as indicating that malaria may mask LF rather than cause mortality independently. The study suggests that parallel assessment, timely specimen collection, and improved diagnostic communication are essential for earlier LF detection. However, the reliance on retrospective data introduces potential recall bias, limiting the confidence in the findings. The evidence is moderate in strength due to these limitations.

title: Assessment of Edo People Attitude Towards Lassa Fever Diseases Prevention Campaign Programme

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study examines the attitudes of Edo people in Owan West Local Government Area (LGA) towards Lassa fever prevention campaigns, particularly those broadcast by KU 92.7 FM. Guided by Behaviour Theory and the Health Belief Model, the research explores how awareness and cultural beliefs influence health behaviours.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Using a survey method, 398 respondents were selected through stratified and random sampling from a projected population of 112,503. The study focuses on the Edo people in Owan West LGA, with an emphasis on their attitudes towards Lassa fever prevention campaigns.
analysis.methods: A survey method was employed, involving stratified and random sampling to select 398 respondents from a projected population of 112,503. The study relied on self-reported data to assess attitudes and awareness of Lassa fever prevention campaigns.
analysis.main_results: Findings reveal a high level of awareness of Lassa fever, largely due to efforts by health organizations such as the NCDC, Edo State Ministry of Health, and Irrua Specialist Hospital. Trust in health professionals was found to enhance campaign effectiveness, though some skepticism persists due to misinformation and cultural beliefs.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Awareness does not consistently lead to preventive action, highlighting gaps in behavioural change. Tailoring communication strategies to local contexts is essential for fostering sustained health behaviour change.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the design of more effective public health messaging and the inclusion of traditional leaders in campaign strategies to improve acceptance and effectiveness of Lassa fever prevention efforts.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on self-reported data and the potential influence of cultural practices on responses. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational nature of the study and the lack of control groups.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the attitudes of the Edo people in Owan West Local Government Area towards Lassa fever prevention campaigns, particularly those broadcast by KU 92.7 FM. It is guided by Behaviour Theory and the Health Belief Model, aiming to understand how awareness and cultural beliefs influence health behaviours. The research employed a survey method, selecting 398 respondents through stratified and random sampling. Results indicate a high level of awareness of Lassa fever, largely attributed to efforts by health organizations. However, awareness does not consistently translate into preventive actions, underscoring gaps in behavioural change. Trust in health professionals was found to enhance campaign effectiveness, yet some skepticism remains due to misinformation and cultural beliefs. The study highlights the importance of tailoring communication strategies to local contexts for sustained health behaviour change. While the findings are informative, the study's reliance on self-reported data and lack of control groups limit the confidence in its conclusions, resulting in moderate evidence strength.
